papers.title: Deciphering tissue architecture with StKAN: A multi-modal deep learning framework combining morphology and spatial transcriptomics.
papers.summary: StKAN is a new deep learning tool that combines tissue morphology (from images) with spatial transcriptomics data to better map out tissue structure. It likely uses Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks (KAN), a newer neural network architecture, to integrate these multi-modal data types more effectively than prior methods. The goal is to improve how researchers identify distinct tissue regions and cell organization patterns directly from combined imaging and gene expression data.
papers.why: This kind of multi-modal framework could be directly applied to integrating spatial transcriptomics with tissue morphology in brain sections, helping to map interneuron subtypes and perineuronal net distributions with much finer spatial resolution.

papers.title: FoxO3a-Smad4 Co-localization and Autophagy Alterations are Associated with Cognitive Impairment in Alcohol-Dependent Rats Fed a High-Fat Diet.
papers.summary: This study looks at rats that were made dependent on alcohol and also fed a high-fat diet, examining how this combination affects the brain. The researchers found that two proteins, FoxO3a and Smad4, appear together (co-localize) in brain cells more under these conditions, and that markers of autophagy (the cell's internal recycling process) were altered. These molecular changes were linked to worse performance on cognitive tests, suggesting a connection between disrupted autophagy signaling and memory or learning problems.
papers.why: This paper is relevant because it links autophagy pathway disruption to cognitive outcomes in a neurological disease model, offering molecular targets and mechanisms that could inform how autophagy dysregulation contributes to neuronal dysfunction relevant to your work on mitophagy/autophagy in brain neurons.

papers.title: Decoding multiple sclerosis: linking autoimmunity, and nutrition/environmental factors to mitochondrial dysfunction and therapeutic opportunities.
papers.summary: This paper explores how multiple sclerosis arises from a combination of autoimmune attacks, environmental and nutritional factors, and mitochondrial dysfunction. It discusses how these elements interact to damage neurons and glial cells, worsening disease progression. The authors also highlight potential therapeutic strategies that target mitochondrial health to help manage or slow the disease.
papers.why: Understanding mitochondrial dysfunction in neurological disease is directly relevant to studying mitophagy and autophagy pathways in neurons, which could inform how similar mechanisms operate in interneuron health and perineuronal net integrity.

papers.title: A double-duty champion: Eurycoma longifolia counters oxidative stress and unlocks autophagy to safeguard neurons and muscle cells.
papers.summary: This paper investigates how Eurycoma longifolia, a medicinal plant extract, protects neurons and muscle cells by reducing oxidative stress and activating autophagy. The research suggests the plant compound has a dual protective mechanism against cellular damage. This could position it as a potential therapeutic agent for conditions involving oxidative stress and impaired autophagy.

papers.title: Mitophagy Facilitates Cytosolic Proteostasis to Preserve Cardiac Function.
papers.summary: This paper investigates how mitophagy, the process of clearing damaged mitochondria, helps maintain proper protein quality control in the cytoplasm of heart cells. The authors show that when mitophagy is impaired, cytosolic proteins fail to fold and degrade properly, leading to proteotoxic stress. This dysfunction ultimately contributes to declining cardiac function, linking mitochondrial quality control to broader cellular proteostasis mechanisms.
papers.why: Although this study focuses on cardiac tissue, the core mechanism connecting mitophagy to cytosolic proteostasis is directly relevant to understanding neuronal mitophagy and its potential downstream effects on protein homeostasis in interneurons.

papers.title: NAD⁺ or β-Hydroxybutyrate Each Protects Against Tachypacing-induced Metabolic Remodeling Through Regulation of Mitophagy in HL-1 Cardiomyocytes.
papers.summary: This study looks at HL-1 cardiomyocytes (a heart muscle cell line) subjected to rapid electrical pacing, which mimics stress seen in atrial fibrillation and causes metabolic remodeling. The researchers found that treating these cells with either NAD⁺ or β-hydroxybutyrate protected them from this metabolic damage. Both compounds appeared to work by regulating mitophagy, the process cells use to clear out damaged mitochondria.
papers.why: Although this paper studies heart cells rather than neurons, its detailed mechanistic insight into how mitophagy regulation protects against metabolic stress could inform hypotheses about mitochondrial quality control pathways relevant to neuronal and interneuron health in the brain.

papers.title: Autophagy and mitophagy in pancreatic β-cell homeostasis and their involvement in diabetes pathophysiology.
papers.summary: This paper reviews how autophagy and mitophagy (the process of clearing damaged mitochondria) help maintain healthy pancreatic beta-cells, which produce insulin. It explains how disruptions in these quality-control pathways can contribute to beta-cell dysfunction and death, key features of diabetes. The review likely covers molecular mechanisms and potential therapeutic angles targeting autophagy/mitophagy in diabetes.
papers.why: While focused on a different cell type, this paper offers transferable mechanistic insight into mitophagy pathway regulation that could inform interpretation of neuronal mitophagy findings in the PhD project.

papers.title: The protection of chitosan-coated triptolide-magnesium nanoparticles against intervertebral disc degeneration via MAPK signaling and mitophagy.
papers.summary: This paper describes chitosan-coated nanoparticles containing triptolide and magnesium designed to treat intervertebral disc degeneration. The nanoparticles appear to work by activating mitophagy (a cellular quality-control process that clears damaged mitochondria) and modulating MAPK signaling pathways. The researchers show this combination protects disc cells from degeneration in their experimental models.
papers.why: While this paper focuses on spinal disc tissue rather than brain neurons, its mechanistic insights into mitophagy regulation via MAPK signaling could offer transferable concepts for understanding mitochondrial quality control pathways relevant to neuronal health and mitophagy research.
